record.paper_title: Conformally invariant scaling limits: an overview and a collection of problems
record.original_question: In critical site percolation on the triangular lattice in the upper half-plane with mesh ε, choose a parameter p(ε) so that the probability of a left-to-right white crossing of a fixed 1×1 square equals a prescribed value q in (0, 1), with q ≠ 1/2. The resulting interface is an unbounded path starting at 0. Determine the scaling limit of this interface as ε tends to 0 under this near-critical tuning of p(ε).

evidence.quote: Suppose that in Figure 3 with small mesh ǫ > 0 we choose p(ǫ) so that the probability to have a left to right crossing of white hexagons in some fixed 1 × 1 square in the upper half plane is q at percolation parameter p = p(ǫ).
Problem 2.10 (Lincoln Chayes (personal communication)). What is the scaling limit of the interface as ǫ ց 0 and p = p(ǫ) if q 6= 1/2 is fixed?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider site percolation on the triangular lattice with mesh ε > 0, restricted to the upper half-plane. Each hexagonal site is independently colored white with probability p and black with probability 1 − p. Fix a 1 × 1 square Q in the upper half-plane and let f(p, ε) denote the probability of a left-to-right white crossing of Q. Fix a value q ∈ (0, 1) with q ≠ 1/2, and for each ε > 0 choose p(ε) so that f(p(ε), ε) = q. With suitable boundary conditions placing white sites on the positive real axis and black sites on the negative real axis, there is an unbounded interface (a simple lattice path) starting at the origin and separating the two colors.

Determine the scaling limit, as ε ↓ 0, of this interface viewed as a random curve in the upper half-plane, under the near-critical tuning p = p(ε) corresponding to fixed crossing probability q ≠ 1/2. In particular, describe whether the limit exists, identify it explicitly (for example as a "massive" or otherwise perturbed variant of SLE₆), and characterize its law.
artifact.status_search_result: The near-critical scaling limit of 2D percolation on the triangular lattice has been substantially developed: Camia–Newman–Fontes described a conjectural framework, and Garban–Pete–Schramm (arXiv:1305.5526) constructed the scaling limit of near-critical percolation in the quad-crossing topology and showed it is invariant under translations but not under rotations/scalings, giving a "massive" deformation of the critical limit. Tuning p(ε) so that a fixed 1×1 crossing probability equals q ≠ 1/2 corresponds to a specific near-critical scale, and the corresponding interface is expected to converge to a "massive SLE₆"-type curve. While the existence and many properties of this near-critical limit are now established, an explicit, fully characterized description of the interface law as a continuum curve (analogous to SLE₆ at criticality) does not appear to have been completely achieved, so the precise problem is best classified as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: The scaling limits of near-critical and dynamical percolation
status_evidence.snippet: We construct the scaling limit of near-critical percolation on the triangular grid as the mesh η → 0, in the quad-crossing space of percolation configurations.
status_evidence.claim: The near-critical scaling limit exists and is constructed, supporting partial resolution of Chayes' question.

status_evidence.title: The Scaling Limit Geometry of Near-Critical 2D Percolation
status_evidence.snippet: Framework combining the continuum nonsimple loop process at criticality with Poissonian marking of macroscopically pivotal sites describes the near-critical scaling limit geometry.
status_evidence.claim: A conjectural geometric description of the near-critical scaling limit has been formulated.

status_evidence.title: Trivial, Critical and Near-critical Scaling Limits of Two-dimensional Percolation
status_evidence.snippet: Three possible types of scaling limits are identified, with the near-critical type corresponding to an intermediate speed of approach of p to p_c.
status_evidence.claim: The near-critical regime is well-understood at the level of qualitative scaling-limit classification.
